title: Food, reflected on
hookLine: one of the forty subjects asks you to like your lunch less. why?
tomorrow: what is your body actually made of?

cards: A sandwich in one hand, a phone in the other, gone before you tasted it. So what does a meditation manual have to say about lunch? Something odd.
In Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, one of the forty meditation subjects is the perception of repulsiveness in food. Practice finding your meal unappealing.
That's a strange thing to ask of anyone, let alone someone who has just been handed it as a gift. Why would a monk train himself to like his lunch less?

teach.h: FOLLOW ONE MEAL ALL THE WAY.
teach.b: Buddhaghosa's answer is a journey. He walks the monk through the whole life of one meal. Leaving the quiet of the monastery, in heat or cold.
Walking to the village. Going house to house with a bowl, past dogs and puddles. Then the chewing, the swallowing, the stomach, and finally where it leaves the body.

teach.h: NOTHING ON THE LIST IS FALSE.
teach.b: Nothing on that list is false. It's food's whole trip, not just the picture of it on a plate.
And the target isn't the food. It's the craving.

teach.h: NOT FOR FUN, BUT TO KEEP GOING.
teach.b: As the perception grows, the manual says, the mind draws back from the hunger for flavors, and the monk eats just to keep going, without fuss or vanity.

There's an older reflection behind this, in the Buddha's discourse on all the taints, chanted before meals in monasteries: I use this food not for fun, not for showing off, not to bulk up or to look good, but to keep this body going, to ease hunger's discomfort, and to support the good life.
So the puzzle comes apart. The strange meditation isn't hate for your lunch. It's seeing the meal whole, field to body, so the grabbing loosens and the eating becomes plain, and even grateful.

how: Theravada monastics recite a reflection on the purpose of food, drawn from the Discourse on All the Taints, before or while eating; the perception of repulsiveness in food is a meditation subject in the Visuddhimagga, taken up with a teacher.

o: a strict diet that cuts out every tasty dish
a meal seen on its whole trip, eaten without craving
a fast kept to make the mind sharp and light

games.q: the meal's journey — tap the pairs.
p: not for fun or to look good

s: the food meditation teaches you to hate your meal
it follows the meal's whole trip so the craving for flavors loosens. the food isn't the enemy.
Buddhaghosa follows the meal all the way through the body
from the walk to the village to the stomach and beyond. nothing on the list is false.
the reflection says to eat for pleasure and good looks
it says the opposite: not for fun, not to look good, but to keep the body going and support the good life.

games.q: a friend says she's trying a meditation that makes her feel guilty every time she enjoys a meal. what would Buddhaghosa's practice say?
o: guilt is the point: the more you dislike food, the better.
the point is loosening craving, not guilt; eat plainly, even gladly.
skip it: meditation shouldn't touch something as ordinary as food.
games.why: the target is craving for flavors, not the meal and not the eater. the monk eats to keep going, without fuss.

practice: Take the last thing you ate and follow it backward: the field or the orchard, the hands that picked it, the truck, the store, your own hands. Then follow it forward, into your body, becoming the next hour of your day.
Keep it plain, no judging, just the trip.

wordCard.voice: Food, reflected on: one of the forty subjects. A meal seen on its whole journey, so it's eaten to keep going, not to feed the craving.

orig.note: Pali: perception of repulsiveness in nutriment, one of the forty meditation subjects.

carryVoice: For the road: food's journey, longer than the minutes it spends on the plate. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 11 (the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment: the aspects of going, seeking, using, secretion, receptacle, the uncooked and cooked, fruit, outflow and smearing; as it grows the mind retreats from craving for flavors and he uses nutriment only to cross over suffering, without vanity)

Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (wisely reflecting, he uses almsfood not for amusement, intoxication, adornment or beautification, but for the endurance of this body, ending discomfort and assisting the holy life)
